To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we detected MRSA in a farmer with cutaneous lesions and also in the pigs on his farm, and that we identified the first lnu(A)-containing MRSA ST398 isolate.
MRSA ST398 is a zoonotic pathogen that can be transmitted between humans and pigs and that it is associated with skin infections in humans.
we detected MRSA-ST398 in a farmer and in his pigs, with a clonal relationship between the human isolate and those from the farm.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the detection of MRSA-ST398 in a farmer, with skin infection and nasal colonization with MRSA-ST398, and the presence of MRSA-ST108 in 11/12 nasal samples of pigs of his farm.
the detection of a MRSA-ST398 clone, with skin infection in a farmer and in pigs of their farm, and the first detection of the lincomycin resistance lnu(A) in ST398.

the first detection of MRSA-ST398 in a farmer and in pigs of a farm in Portugal, and the first detection in MRSA-ST98 of the lnuA gene, which was associated with the presence of lincomycin-resistant isolates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the patient was infected by the MRSA strain that was present in the nasal cavity of the pigs, which was the same strain that was present on the skin of the farmer, and that the lnu(A)-positive MRSA strain was transmitted from the pigs to the farmer.
the farmer was infected by MRSA-ST398 of swine origin.
the farmer and his pigs were co-infected by the same MRSA clone, which is the most frequent MRSA clone in pigs and humans in the Netherlands.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown a possible pig to human transfer of a MRSA-ST398 strain with the lnu(A)-gene.
the lnu(A)-carrying MRSA-ST398 was detected in the nasal samples of the farmer and his pigs, and the same strain was detected in his skin lesions.
the lnu(A)-positive MRSA-ST398 strains detected in a pig farmer and his pigs were clonally related.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of MRSA in the nasal cavity of pigs is not necessarily a risk factor for the development of MRSA infection in humans.
MRSA ST398 has become an important cause of human infections in many countries.
MRSA-ST398 has been isolated from a farmer with skin infections, and from the pigs on his farm, which suggests a potential pig-to-human translocation of MRSA.
